Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images World news US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over Greenland The agreement would allow the US to expand its military presence, while Denmark and Greenland say it preserves their sovereignty and right to self-determination Robert Mackey Fri 18 Sep 2026 21.01 EDT First published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for much of his second term to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force. The full scope of the deal Trump described as “very important, historic, and special” was not immediately clear. But soon after his announcement in a post on Truth Social, the leaders of Denmark and Greenland issued statements indicating the deal would be signed by the three governments on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City next week. Trump renews call for US to take over Greenland as he arrives for Nato summit Read more In his social media post, Trump cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming that the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”. “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato . The announcement comes just weeks before November’s midterms, giving the president a foreign policy accomplishment he can tout to voters as the deeply unpopular war with Iran becomes an increasing political liability for Republicans vying to hang on to their narrow majorities in the House and Senate. The US has long had a military presence in Greenland – a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member – and has had a military base at Pituffik since the cold war. In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”. Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late on Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s previously stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”. Frederiksen said that what she called “a great agreement” for all three parties “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. Nielsen said it was “joyous” that the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base. Once agreed to, the pact would need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the Danish and Greenlandic statements said. Earlier in his term, Trump argued that the US needed control of Greenland for “economic security” , and has described ownership and control of the territory as an “absolute necessity”. The island had long been on the president’s radar as a target for purchase, and during his first term, in 2019, Trump confirmed reports he had been urging aides to find out how the US could buy Greenland, describing any sale as “essentially a large real estate deal”. Trump’s claims deepened divisions among the western alliance, with the Danish government repeatedly stating that Greenland was “not for sale”. When concerns over Trump’s annexation threats reached a fever pitch last year, the Guardian reported that the Danish government set up a “night watch” in the foreign ministry to monitor the US president’s pronouncements while Copenhagen sleeps. At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland. He threatened to pull all American armed forces out of Europe after the continent repeatedly pushed back. Strategically positioned between the US and Russia, Greenland is viewed as increasingly important for defense and is emerging as a geopolitical battleground as Arctic ice melts. The US vice-president, JD Vance, and his wife Usha, received a frosty reception when they visited US troops stationed at Pituffik space base last year, amid the White House’s aggressive campaign to take the mineral-rich island with roughly 56,000 inhabitants. Polling has found Greenlanders strongly oppose any effort to make Greenland a part of the US. Even so, a Trump administration insider dropped a hint online that the US side intends to present whatever the deal actually is as an American triumph. Katie Miller, a former White House aide whose husband is Trump’s closest adviser, posted a map of Greenland covered in the American flag, with the caption: “ITS [sic] HAPPENING”. https://www.politico.eu/article/france-e.text: BRUSSELS ― Political pressure is leaving Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz poorly placed to break the deadlock over the EU’s next seven-year budget. As EU leaders gather for a two-day summit in Brussels from Thursday, the heads of the bloc's two largest countries hold the keys to breaking the impasse between capitals that has persisted for months, as a Germany-led group advocating a smaller budget clashes with those like France which are resisting reductions. "Delays and persisting divisions in the Council [representing EU governments] are worrying," said Siegfried Mureșan, co-leading the European Parliament's work on the MFF, the multiannual financial framework. "The EU budget can only be built through compromise ... The faster we adopt the budget, the faster we can implement it and become more competitive, safer, help farmers and researchers and protect our borders and cyberspace." Advertisement Advertisement Sealing agreement on the EU's long-term central budget, worth approximately €2 trillion, is the biggest challenge over the next few months facing leaders, all of whom must sign up to the final numbers. While it isn't just up to Macron and Merz, getting the chiefs of the bloc's two most powerful countries to overcome their differences would be a massive step in making all the pieces of the jigsaw slot into place. But with Macron soon to leave office and Merz under severe pressure domestically, officials and diplomats in Brussels, Paris, and Berlin are playing down hopes of a Franco-German breakthrough this week. "If the French and German leaders come hand in hand, I think that could change the game," an EU diplomat, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said. "You need [Italian Prime Minister Giorgia] Meloni and [Polish Prime Minister Donald] Tusk, but it starts with Merz and Macron." While Merz and Macron may talk bilaterally during the summit, according to an Elysée official, there were no firm plans for a more formal sit-down, two EU diplomats said, adding they were expecting them to use the two-day meeting to hash out positions. Domestic political weakness makes both leaders less likely to yield ground, three EU diplomats said. Backfiring For the French president, who leaves office next year, the fear is that making big concessions — like accepting cuts demanded by Berlin — could be weaponized by presidential candidates vying to replace him. “Macron should not appear too conciliatory” in budget talks, said an ally of the French president. “It would backfire in the presidential campaign.” Advertisement Advertisement Indeed, Macron may be wary of striking a deal that could lead to attacks from far-right leader Marine Le Pen or far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon, both of whom argue that France receives too little value for its contributions to the EU pot. During a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday evening, Le Pen accused negotiators of speeding up talks as "an attempt to stifle future democratic choices before they even take place" — effectively warning Macron against locking in an agreement before France's April presidential election and votes in other major EU countries, such as Spain, which goes to the polls next month, and Italy, which is due to hold a poll next year. "All this is not serious," Le Pen told reporters on the 26th floor of The Hotel in Brussels. It's complicated Merz faces similar political pressures. Following humiliating state election defeats to the far-right Alternative for Germany party, the Chancellor is wary of concessions that could be framed as sending more taxpayer money to Brussels. Berlin prefers no deal at all to one that increases the overall budget, Merz said. But Paris and Berlin's positions may not be as far apart as public statements suggest. Advertisement Advertisement "It’s complicated because France and Germany both need to step outside of their comfort zone," said the Macron ally. "But it will end with a deal between France and Germany," France's Europe minister Benjamin Haddad told reporters on Tuesday that discussions should focus on raising money via taxes, or "own resources" as they're known in the EU —such as online gambling levies—rather than "massive cuts." However, Paris also wants to "stabilize national contributions" ― in other words, keep its own payments level. Berlin was "open to examine new own resources, but we are more skeptical than the French that it will generate enough money," a German official said. France is betting that when push comes to shove, Merz will give in to pressure from other countries — and German captains of industry — to abandon his demands for far-reaching cuts. “I see that there is also a real debate in Germany as well on the fact of having a position that would only be focused on cuts to the detriment of future policies,” an Elysée official said Wednesday. This week, Germany’s industrial lobby BDI and top industry groups urged their government to defend a more ambitious EU budget. Advertisement Advertisement Macron and Merz showed unity earlier this month by jointly urging the European Commission to toughen its stance on China. But they still struggle to agree on another major deal— first reported by POLITICO in July —where Berlin accepts stronger "Made in Europe" rules in exchange for France backing relaxed car emission targets and the 2035 combustion engine ban. EU Industry chief Stéphane Séjourné told POLITICO on Tuesday he supported the deal to finalize both files. Macron recently called the agreement “imminent,” suggesting progress depended on German coalition talks. But their failure to present an agreement at this week’s Paris car show confirms Paris and Berlin still disagree on terms, with the Elysée confirming negotiations remain ongoing.

https://baltic-review.com/wroclaw-water-.text: Share Tweet 0 Wrocław’s Oder riverfront reflects the close relationship between urban life, water management and natural space. Wrocław will become a meeting point for Poland’s water, urban-planning and environmental communities next week, when the eighth City–Water–Quality of Life Congress takes place on 13–14 October 2026. The programme is built around a practical question: how can cities manage water and natural assets in ways that improve everyday life while preparing for a changing climate? The announcement, published by the University of Łódź on 9 October, presents the congress as a forum for scientists, local-government representatives, policymakers, businesses and independent experts. Its three guiding themes are city, water and quality of life, linking technical infrastructure with public space, environmental policy and the social experience of urban life. ([uni.lodz.pl](https://www.uni.lodz.pl/en/news/details/8th-city-water-quality-of-life-congress-with-the-participation-of-a-unilodz-researcher?utm_source=openai)) From water infrastructure to natural capital Among the subjects on the agenda are urban water retention, the modernisation of water-supply systems, critical infrastructure, hydrological management technologies and the role of nature in city planning. The programme also gives space to the idea of “natural capital”: the value provided by parks, wetlands, river valleys and other ecosystems that are often treated as background scenery rather than as part of a city’s essential infrastructure. A dedicated discussion on 14 October will ask how Polish cities can account for nature when making planning and investment decisions. The session will be moderated by Iwona Wagner, an associate professor at the University of Łódź and co-organiser of the congress. Participants listed for the panel include representatives of Wrocław, Kraków, the University of Warsaw, the Institute of Urban and Regional Development and the Wrocław Technology Park. ([uni.lodz.pl](https://www.uni.lodz.pl/en/news/details/8th-city-water-quality-of-life-congress-with-the-participation-of-a-unilodz-researcher?utm_source=openai)) The subject is increasingly relevant to cities whose residents experience water in several ways at once: as a resource, a landscape feature, a transport and recreation corridor, and a source of planning challenges. A riverfront may support biodiversity and public life, but the same urban water system must also cope with intense rainfall, periods of scarcity, ageing infrastructure and competing demands from households, businesses and public services. A Wrocław-based platform with a wider reach The congress is being organised by the City of Wrocław, the municipal water company MPWiK Wrocław, the Foundation for Economy and Public Administration and Wrocław University of Science and Technology. The event is scheduled for the university’s Congress Centre and will also be available online, with participation offered free of charge subject to registration. ([uni.lodz.pl](https://www.uni.lodz.pl/en/news/details/8th-city-water-quality-of-life-congress-with-the-participation-of-a-unilodz-researcher?utm_source=openai)) Wrocław’s municipal water company describes the congress as a long-running platform focused on the relationship between aquatic and urban environments and their influence on quality of life. Its programme connects water policy with climate adaptation, urban heat, rapid flooding, water demand and the use of waterfront areas to support health and liveability. ([mpwik.wroc.pl](https://www.mpwik.wroc.pl/aktualnosci/?utm_source=openai)) That combination gives the event a distinctly applied character. Rather than treating climate resilience solely as an engineering issue, the congress places it alongside urban design, public administration, education and the protection of ecological functions. It also creates a setting in which municipal officials can compare approaches with researchers and infrastructure specialists. Why the discussion matters for Polish cities Polish cities differ greatly in geography and scale, but many face similar questions: where should rainwater be held, how can rivers and wetlands be protected, and how should green areas be included in long-term investment decisions? The answers affect housing, transport, public health, recreation and the cost of maintaining infrastructure. The congress is also expected to present the Water City Index 2026, a ranking of Polish cities’ approaches to water management. Such comparisons can help turn a broad sustainability debate into a more concrete conversation about indicators, investment priorities and local performance. ([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/tanja-iamwater_honoured-to-be-among-the-first-announced-activity-7491201576389275648-aPGB?utm_source=openai)) For Wrocław, the event continues a civic and institutional interest in the city’s relationship with water. For participants from other regions, it offers an opportunity to examine how river valleys, parks and wetlands can be treated not simply as constraints on development, but as assets that support healthier and more adaptable urban environments. With the congress beginning on Tuesday, 13 October, the immediate focus will be on exchanging evidence and practical experience. Its broader message is straightforward: water management, nature protection and the quality of urban life are increasingly part of the same planning conversation.
